britannica-1911-heemskerk-martin-jacobsz:
Martin Jacobsz Heemskerk (1498–1574) was a Dutch painter. He was born at Heemskerk in Holland in 1498. His farmer father apprenticed him to a Haarlem painter. The father recalled him to the plough after a time. The boy ran away at the first chance. He walked fifty miles to Delft in a single day. Haarlem's John Schoreel became his real master there.

Italy occupied his wandering years afterward. At Rome he helped decorate triumphal arches for Charles V in 1536. Vasari praised his battle-pieces from that work. Haarlem gave him its guild presidency in 1540. Practice there was large and lucrative for decades. He fled Haarlem's Spanish siege in 1572 for Amsterdam. His preserved will shows he had made a fortune. He left money to Haarlem's orphanage in trust. The interest rewards couples who marry on his tomb. He died on 1 October 1574.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacob-corneli:
Dutch painter Jacob Cornelisz worked in the first third of the sixteenth century. He is also called Jacob van Amsterdam or van Oostzann. He is sometimes confused with Walter van Assen. Nothing certain is known about his life or his links to other artists. He was among the last Dutch painters untouched by Italian influence.

His pupil Jan van Scorel, by contrast, became the first Romanist. Cornelisz composed naturally, with agreeable feeling in the old Flemish manner. His colors are rich and warm. His backgrounds show attractive landscapes. Yet drawing errors and an ugly realism often mar his work. Surviving pictures date from 1506 to 1530. A small Berlin altarpiece shows Madonna and Child with music-making angels. The entry presents a late Flemish painter on the edge of change.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jan-dlugosz:
Eminent medieval Polish historian Jan Dlugosz, in Latin Longinus, was born at Brzeznica in 1415. He died at Cracow on 19 May 1480. He was one of twelve sons of John and Beata. He received primary schooling at Nowy Korczyn, then entered Cracow Academy, studying literature and philosophy. He was ordained priest in 1440 and became secretary to Cardinal Zbigniew Olesnicki, bishop of Cracow. Later he became a cathedral prelate and tutor to King Casimir IV's children.

He served as Polish royal ambassador to foreign lands, especially Bohemia and Hungary, settling political disturbances there. Church superiors sent him as representative to Pope Eugenius IV and as delegate to Basel council. He declined Prague's archbishopric, but shortly before death was named archbishop of Lemberg. Dlugosz spent his great industry on a vast history of Poland. The entry presents a priest-diplomat who became his nation's chronicler.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jan-ingen-hou:
Plant physiologist, physicist, and physician Jan Ingen-Housz was born at Breda, North Brabant, on 8 December 1730. He died at London on 7 September 1799. He attended Breda's Latin school, then studied medicine, physics, and chemistry at Louvain and Leyden. He earned a doctorate in medicine, though when and where remain unknown. From 1757 he practiced medicine at Breda. After his father's death, and at royal physician John Pringle's invitation, he settled in London in 1765.

There he met William Hunter, Alexander Monro, and George Armstrong. Under Armstrong he studied smallpox inoculation of children, then a new theory, and became its zealous advocate. In spring 1768 he was called to Vienna to inoculate the imperial family. He succeeded despite hostility from Viennese physician Anton de Haen. The entry presents a Dutch physician whose plant studies showed green leaves giving off oxygen under light.
